# Validation of the proper binormal fit

This report checks `smooth(method = "proper")` (issue
#152) against the published results of the "proper" binormal model (PBM). It
is maintainer-only: knit it from the package root with the version of pROC
to check installed, and mvtnorm:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
rmarkdown::render("tools/proper_binormal_validation.Rmd")
# or with fewer datasets, on one core (Windows):
rmarkdown::render("tools/proper_binormal_validation.Rmd", params = list(B = 200, cores = 1))
```

With `B = 2000` datasets per simulated population it takes about 2 hours on 4
cores.

Sources:

- **M&P**: Metz CE, Pan X (1999) "Proper" binormal ROC curves: theory and
  maximum-likelihood estimation. *J Math Psychol* 43:1–33.
- **P&M**: Pesce LL, Metz CE (2007) Reliable and computationally efficient
  maximum-likelihood estimation of "proper" binormal ROC curves. *Acad
  Radiol* 14:814–829.
- **Owen**: Owen DB (1956) Tables for computing bivariate normal
  probabilities. *Ann Math Stat* 27:1075–1090.

```{r setup}
library(pROC)
library(parallel)
B <- params$B
cores <- params$cores
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(20261103)
# AUC of the least-squares binormal line, as smooth(method = "binormal") of
# pROC 1.19 computed it; NA where it refused the curve
ls.auc <- function(r) {
  df <- data.frame(sp = qnorm(r$specificities), se = qnorm(r$sensitivities))
  df <- df[is.finite(df$sp) & is.finite(df$se), ]
  df <- df[c(TRUE, diff(df$sp) != 0 | diff(df$se) != 0), ]
  if (nrow(df) <= 1 || pROC:::smooth_roc_binormal_degenerate(df)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  co <- coefficients(lm(sp ~ se, df))
  unname(pnorm(co[1] / sqrt(1 + co[2]^2)))
}
c(pROC = as.character(packageVersion("pROC")), mvtnorm = as.character(packageVersion("mvtnorm")), R = R.version.string)
```

## AUC (M&P Eq. 36)

The AUC of the PBM is computed with M&P p. 12, Eq. 36. P&M Table 1 (p. 826)
lists the curve parameters of 9 population curves of known AUC, to 6
significant digits:

```{r eq36}
table1 <- data.frame(
  auc = rep(c(0.6, 0.85, 0.95), each = 3),
  shape = rep(c("high", "medium", "symmetric"), 3),
  da = c(0.1, 0.358, 0.358287, 1.24365, 1.46571, 1.46574, 0.0999998, 2.324, 2.32618),
  c = c(-0.154357, -0.046907, 0, -0.428571, -0.14, 0, -0.853738, -0.292369, 0)
)
table1$eq36 <- mapply(pROC:::proper_binormal_auc, table1$da, table1$c)
knitr::kable(table1, digits = 8)
```

The largest difference to the published AUCs is
`r signif(max(abs(table1$eq36 - table1$auc)), 2)`, within the rounding of the
parameters.

At $d_a = 0$, $F(0, 0; \rho) = 1/4 + \arcsin(\rho) / (2\pi)$ (Owen p. 1078),
so the AUC is $1 + \arcsin(\rho) / \pi$ with $\rho = -(1 - c^2) / (1 + c^2)$:

```{r closed-form}
cs <- c(-0.99, -0.5, -1e-3, -1e-6, 1e-6, 1e-3, 0.5, 0.99)
closed <- 1 + asin(-(1 - cs^2) / (1 + cs^2)) / pi
max(abs(vapply(cs, pROC:::proper_binormal_auc, numeric(1), da = 0) - closed))
```

## Continuous data (P&M Tables 2–4)

P&M p. 822 generate continuous data from the PBM: $x$ from the conventional
binormal model with parameters $a$ and $b$ (negatives $N(0, 1)$, positives
$N(a / b, 1 / b)$), and $y = -[(bx - a)^2 - x^2] / 2$, the decision variable
of the PBM (M&P Eq. 11). $a$ and $b$ follow from $d_a$ and $c$ (M&P p. 23). At
$c = 0$ ($b = 1$), $y$ is linear in $x$, which is used directly.

For each of the 9 population curves of Table 1, `r B` datasets of 50 negative
and 50 positive cases are fitted with `method = "proper"`, and, for comparison,
with the least-squares binormal fit (`method = "binormal"` of pROC 1.19, `ls.auc()` above) and the
empirical AUC. Data with perfect performance (see below) give the limit
AUC = 1, which is kept in the means as an estimate, as PROPROC returns it;
`perfect` counts them.

```{r continuous, cache = TRUE}
sim.pbm <- function(n, da, c) {
  b <- (1 + c) / (1 - c)
  a <- da * sqrt(1 + c^2) / (1 - c)
  y <- if (c == 0) identity else function(x) -((b * x - a)^2 - x^2) / 2
  list(controls = y(rnorm(n)), cases = y(rnorm(n, a / b, 1 / b)))
}
fit.auc <- function(d) {
  r <- roc(controls = d$controls, cases = d$cases, direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  s <- tryCatch(smooth(r, method = "proper"), error = function(e) NULL)
  c(
    proper = if (is.null(s)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(auc(s)),
    # perfect performance: the limit AUC = 1, without a log-likelihood
    perfect = !is.null(s) && is.na(s$proper$logLik),
    lm = ls.auc(r),
    empirical = as.numeric(auc(r))
  )
}
# P&M Tables 2-4 (pp. 826-827), 50 positive and 50 negative cases: mean AUC
# and empirical SD of the estimates
published <- data.frame(
  mean = c(0.617, 0.610, 0.608, 0.860, 0.852, 0.852, 0.957, 0.951, 0.951),
  sd = c(0.049, 0.050, 0.051, 0.034, 0.038, 0.038, 0.018, 0.021, 0.019)
)
continuous <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(table1)), function(i) {
  do.call(rbind, mclapply(seq_len(B), function(j) {
    fit.auc(sim.pbm(50, table1$da[i], table1$c[i]))
  }, mc.cores = cores))
})
summary.continuous <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(continuous), function(i) {
  p <- continuous[[i]][, "proper"]
  n <- sum(!is.na(p))
  data.frame(
    auc = table1$auc[i], shape = table1$shape[i],
    mean = mean(p, na.rm = TRUE), se = sd(p, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n),
    published = published$mean[i],
    sd = sd(p, na.rm = TRUE), published.sd = published$sd[i],
    perfect = sum(continuous[[i]][, "perfect"]), failures = sum(is.na(p))
  )
}))
summary.continuous$z <- (summary.continuous$mean - summary.continuous$published) / summary.continuous$se
knitr::kable(summary.continuous, digits = c(2, 0, 4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 0, 0, 1))
```

### Bias, and comparison with the least-squares fit

```{r bias}
bias <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(continuous), function(i) {
  res <- continuous[[i]]
  true <- table1$auc[i]
  rmse <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - true)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  data.frame(
    auc = true, shape = table1$shape[i],
    bias.proper = mean(res[, "proper"], na.rm = TRUE) - true,
    bias.published = published$mean[i] - true,
    bias.lm = mean(res[, "lm"], na.rm = TRUE) - true,
    bias.empirical = mean(res[, "empirical"]) - true,
    rmse.proper = rmse(res[, "proper"]), rmse.lm = rmse(res[, "lm"]), rmse.empirical = rmse(res[, "empirical"]),
    failures.lm = sum(is.na(res[, "lm"]))
  )
}))
knitr::kable(bias, digits = c(2, 0, 4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 0))
```

## Five-category data (M&P Tables 1–3)

M&P sample 1000 datasets of 30 negative and 40 positive cases (p. 21) from the
conventional binormal model with $a = 1.5$ and $b = 0.8$, in 5 categories
with the population operating points (p. 20) (FPF, TPF) = (0.00025, 0.10),
(0.000328, 0.25), (0.03040, 0.50) and (0.28114, 0.85). The FPF 0.000328 is
not on the curve: a TPF of 0.25 needs an FPF of 0.00328. The cut-points are
taken from the TPFs.

```{r five-category, cache = TRUE}
a <- 1.5
b <- 0.8
cuts <- sort((a - qnorm(c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.85))) / b)
fpf.at <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
true.tpf <- pnorm(a + b * qnorm(fpf.at))
true.area <- pnorm(a / sqrt(1 + b^2))
categorical <- do.call(rbind, mclapply(seq_len(B), function(j) {
  r <- roc(
    controls = findInterval(rnorm(30), cuts), cases = findInterval(rnorm(40, a / b, 1 / b), cuts),
    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
  )
  lm.area <- ls.auc(r)
  s <- tryCatch(smooth(r, method = "proper"), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(s)) {
    return(c(rep(NA_real_, 8), lm.area, FALSE))
  }
  c(
    approx(1 - s$specificities, s$sensitivities, xout = fpf.at, ties = max)$y, as.numeric(auc(s)), lm.area,
    is.na(s$proper$logLik)
  )
}, mc.cores = cores))
fitted <- !is.na(categorical[, 8])
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  FPF = fpf.at, true.TPF = true.tpf, mean.TPF = colMeans(categorical[fitted, 1:7]),
  published.mean = c(0.615, 0.705, 0.802, 0.857, 0.921, 0.960, 0.988),
  RMSE = sqrt(colMeans(sweep(categorical[fitted, 1:7], 2, true.tpf)^2)),
  published.RMSE = c(0.1557, 0.1150, 0.0795, 0.0639, 0.0459, 0.0297, 0.0111)
), digits = c(2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4))
```

The area under the proper fits averages
`r round(mean(categorical[fitted, 8]), 4)` (RMSE
`r round(sqrt(mean((categorical[fitted, 8] - true.area)^2)), 4)`), for a true
area of `r round(true.area, 4)` (M&P Table 3, p. 23: 0.879, RMSE 0.0437);
`r sum(categorical[, 10])` of `r B` datasets had perfect performance (AUC = 1),
and `r sum(!fitted)` could not be fitted. The least-squares fit
refuses `r sum(is.na(categorical[, 9]))` of them (degenerate data, or fewer than
two points), with an area of `r round(mean(categorical[, 9], na.rm = TRUE), 4)`
(RMSE `r round(sqrt(mean((categorical[, 9] - true.area)^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)`)
on the others.

## Perfect performance

No curve parameters can be estimated from perfectly separated data (M&P
p. 27), nor, more generally, from data whose operating points all have
FPF = 0 or TPF = 1 (for instance ties straddling a separation): the
likelihood is maximal only in the limit of an AUC of 1. As PROPROC (see
below), pROC then returns that limit, $d_a = 0$ and $c = 1$, with a warning.
Without fitting, the probability that all the controls are below all the
cases, and, for the five-category data, the probability of the more general
case:

```{r separation, cache = TRUE}
N <- 2e5
high <- table1[table1$auc == 0.95 & table1$shape == "high", ]
b.high <- (1 + high$c) / (1 - high$c)
a.high <- high$da * sqrt(1 + high$c^2) / (1 - high$c)
y.high <- function(x) -((b.high * x - a.high)^2 - x^2) / 2
p.high <- mean(replicate(N, max(y.high(rnorm(50))) < min(y.high(rnorm(50, a.high / b.high, 1 / b.high)))))
p.categorical <- mean(replicate(N, max(findInterval(rnorm(30), cuts)) < min(findInterval(rnorm(40, a / b, 1 / b), cuts))))
perfect <- function() {
  k <- tabulate(findInterval(rnorm(30), cuts) + 1, 5)
  l <- tabulate(findInterval(rnorm(40, a / b, 1 / b), cuts) + 1, 5)
  all(rev(cumsum(rev(k)))[-1] == 0 | cumsum(l)[-5] == 0)
}
p.perfect <- mean(replicate(N, perfect()))
c(continuous.0.95.high = p.high, five.category = p.categorical, five.category.perfect = p.perfect) * B
```

These are the expected numbers of such datasets per `r B`.

## Comparison with PROPROC fits

PROPROC itself is no longer distributed, but the repository of the book
*The RJafroc Book: ROC analysis* by Chakraborty (dpc10ster/RJafrocRocBook on
GitHub) keeps the output of PROPROC (OR-DBM MRMC 2.5, version of 2014) for
236 fits, every modality and reader of 14 reader-study datasets, with the
input files (`R/compare-3-fits/MRMCRuns`). They are fitted here again with
`method = "proper"`. For each fit, the log-likelihood that PROPROC's
$(d_a, c)$ can reach is its maximum over the cut-points (`ll.proproc`),
which is compared with pROC's maximum (`ll`).

```{r proproc, cache = TRUE}
commit <- "98aa3ac0a629f63cbb86ca86761e509c80955721"
url <- sprintf("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dpc10ster/RJafrocRocBook/%s/R/compare-3-fits/MRMCRuns", commit)
datasets <- c("DOB1", "DOB2", "DOB3", "FED", "FR", "FZR", "JT", "MAG", "NICO", "OPT", "PEN", "RUS", "TONY", "VD")
# .lrc files: a title line, the ID of the first reader, the modality names,
# the direction of each modality (L: larger values are more positive); then
# per reader the controls (one column per modality), "*", the cases, "*",
# and the ID of the next reader, or "#" at the end
read.lrc <- function(lines) {
  stopifnot(all(strsplit(trimws(lines[4]), "\\s+")[[1]] == "L"))
  readers <- list()
  i <- 5
  block <- function() {
    end <- i + which(trimws(lines[i:length(lines)]) == "*")[1] - 2
    values <- strsplit(trimws(lines[i:end]), "\\s+")
    i <<- end + 2
    do.call(rbind, lapply(values, function(x) as.numeric(x[!grepl("[A-Za-z]", x)])))
  }
  repeat {
    readers[[length(readers) + 1]] <- list(controls = block(), cases = block())
    if (trimws(lines[i]) == "#") break
    i <- i + 1
  }
  readers
}
proproc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(datasets, function(d) {
  data <- read.lrc(readLines(sprintf("%s/%s/%s.lrc", url, d, d)))
  out <- read.csv(sprintf("%s/%s/%sproprocareapooled.csv", url, d, d), strip.white = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(out)), function(j) {
    r <- roc(
      controls = data[[out$R[j]]]$controls[, out$T[j]], cases = data[[out$R[j]]]$cases[, out$T[j]],
      direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
    )
    categories <- pROC:::proper_binormal_categories(r)
    s <- smooth(r, method = "proper")
    data.frame(
      dataset = d, modality = out$T[j], reader = out$R[j], code = out$returnCode[j],
      categories.proproc = out$numCAT[j], categories = length(categories$controls),
      auc.proproc = out$area[j], auc = as.numeric(auc(s)),
      da.proproc = out$d_a[j], da = s$proper$da, c.proproc = out$c[j], c = s$proper$c,
      ll.proproc = if (out$returnCode[j] == 3) NA else
        pROC:::proper_binormal_profile(out$d_a[j], out$c[j], categories$controls, categories$cases),
      ll = s$proper$logLik
    )
  }))
}))
proproc$ll.diff <- proproc$ll - proproc$ll.proproc
proproc$auc.diff <- proproc$auc - proproc$auc.proproc
c(
  fits = nrow(proproc), same.categories = sum(proproc$categories == proproc$categories.proproc),
  same.auc.1e.4 = sum(abs(proproc$auc.diff) < 1e-4),
  ll.lower = sum(proproc$ll.diff < -1e-4, na.rm = TRUE), ll.higher = sum(proproc$ll.diff > 1e-4, na.rm = TRUE),
  da.below.0.01.proproc = sum(proproc$da.proproc < 0.01), da.below.0.01 = sum(proproc$da < 0.01)
)
summary(proproc$ll.diff)
summary(abs(proproc$auc.diff))
mean(proproc$auc.diff)
```

Eq. 36 (pROC's AUC) at PROPROC's own estimates, against PROPROC's AUC:

```{r proproc-eq36}
max(abs(mapply(pROC:::proper_binormal_auc, proproc$da.proproc, proproc$c.proproc) - proproc$auc.proproc))
```

The fits whose AUC differs by more than 1e-4, at the chance line, or with
return code 3 (perfect separation):

```{r proproc-table}
knitr::kable(
  proproc[which(abs(proproc$auc.diff) > 1e-4 | abs(proproc$auc - 0.5) < 1e-3 | proproc$code == 3), c(
    "dataset", "modality", "reader", "code", "auc.proproc", "auc", "da.proproc", "da",
    "c.proproc", "c", "ll.diff"
  )],
  digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3), row.names = FALSE
)
```

## Discussion

```{r z, echo = FALSE}
d <- summary.continuous$mean - summary.continuous$published
se.published <- sqrt(summary.continuous$se^2 + summary.continuous$published.sd^2 / 20000)
z.published <- sum(d / se.published) / 3
z.rounded <- sum(d / sqrt(se.published^2 + 0.0005^2 / 3)) / 3
z.down <- sum((d - 0.0005) / se.published) / 3
```

**Eq. 36.** The AUCs of the 9 population curves of P&M Table 1 agree to
the rounding of their parameters, and the closed form at $d_a = 0$ to machine
precision.

**Continuous data.** All 9 means are above the published ones, by
`r sprintf("%.4f", min(summary.continuous$mean - summary.continuous$published))`
to
`r sprintf("%.4f", max(summary.continuous$mean - summary.continuous$published))`
(`r sprintf("%.1f", min(summary.continuous$z))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(summary.continuous$z))` SE; combined
$z = \sum z / \sqrt{9} =$ `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(summary.continuous$z) / 3)`).
The published means come from 20,000 datasets each (P&M p. 826, note to
Table 2) and are rounded to 3 decimals. With their simulation error, the
combined $z$ is `r sprintf("%.1f", z.published)`; adding the rounding as a
uniform error of $\pm 0.0005$, `r sprintf("%.1f", z.rounded)`; and if all
the published means were rounded down by 0.0005,
`r sprintf("%.1f", z.down)`.

The difference may still be systematic, but it is at most
`r sprintf("%.2f", max((summary.continuous$mean - summary.continuous$published) / summary.continuous$sd))`
SD of the estimates. It is unlikely to come from the fit: on the
reader-study data below, pROC reproduces the fits of a later PROPROC, with a
mean AUC difference of
`r sprintf("%.5f", mean(proproc$auc.diff))`. Nor from the AUC: Eq. 36 at
PROPROC's estimates gives its AUCs within
`r sprintf("%.0e", max(abs(mapply(pROC:::proper_binormal_auc, proproc$da.proproc, proproc$c.proproc) - proproc$auc.proproc)))`.
Nor from the categories: those data have few categories, but P&M's
algorithm uses the truth-run categories of continuous data unchanged up to
400 categories (p. 817), and 50 + 50 cases give at most 100, as in pROC. The
original PROPROC collapsed them into at most 10 or 20, which P&M found
"biases the estimates in a complicated, almost unpredictable, way" (p. 817).
What remains is a detail of the data generation that P&M do not give, or
chance. The SDs agree with the published ones within
`r round(100 * max(abs(summary.continuous$sd / summary.continuous$published.sd - 1)))`%.

**Bias.** The proper fit overestimates the AUC by up to
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(bias$bias.proper))`, most at low AUC and high skew,
like the published fits. P&M (pp. 825–826) attribute it to the lower bound
of 0.5 on the AUC of proper models and to the bounds on the curve shape.
The least-squares fit and the empirical AUC are nearly unbiased on these data (within
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(c(bias$bias.lm, bias$bias.empirical))))`). The
proper fit nevertheless has the lowest RMSE in
`r sum(bias$rmse.proper < pmin(bias$rmse.lm, bias$rmse.empirical))` of the 9
populations, and is within 1% of the least-squares fit in the others (AUC
0.85, symmetric and medium skew). Its advantage is largest at AUC 0.95 with
high skew, where the least-squares fit also refuses
`r bias$failures.lm[bias$auc == 0.95 & bias$shape == "high"]` datasets.

**Five-category data.** The mean TPFs agree with M&P Table 1 within 0.002,
their RMSEs with Table 2 within 2%, and the area with Table 3. The
least-squares fit refuses `r sum(is.na(categorical[, 9]))` of the `r B`
datasets, and underestimates the area of the others.

**Perfect performance and failures.** The proper fit returned the limit
AUC = 1 for `r sum(summary.continuous$perfect)` of the
`r format(9 * B, big.mark = ",")` continuous datasets and for
`r sum(categorical[, 10])` of the `r B` five-category datasets, about the
numbers expected above. It failed on
`r sum(summary.continuous$failures)` continuous and `r sum(!fitted)`
five-category datasets.

**PROPROC.** pROC finds the same categories as PROPROC in
`r sum(proproc$categories == proproc$categories.proproc)` of the
`r nrow(proproc)` reader-study fits, and the same AUC within 1e-4 in
`r sum(abs(proproc$auc.diff) < 1e-4)`, including the fit at the chance line
and the limit AUC = 1 of the perfectly separated data (return code 3, which
PROPROC also uses for these data with a tie straddling the separation).
PROPROC's estimates of $d_a$ are below 0.01 in
`r sum(proproc$da.proproc < 0.01)` fits (mostly about 1e-4, the fits with
return code 6), pROC's in `r sum(proproc$da < 0.01)`: there the
log-likelihood is nearly flat in $d_a$ (P&M p. 820), and both reach the same
maximum. In `r sum(proproc$ll.diff < -1e-4, na.rm = TRUE)` fit, PROPROC finds
a higher maximum
(`r sprintf("%.4f", -min(proproc$ll.diff, na.rm = TRUE))` in log-likelihood)
that pROC's starts miss, with an AUC
`r sprintf("%.3f", -proproc$auc.diff[which.min(proproc$ll.diff)])` higher.

Not covered here: on harder data with many categories, the code review found
maxima that the starts miss, in 2 of 40 samples, with log-likelihoods
0.05 above the fit.
